elements.quote: Our results indicate that PoCUS use contributes to early diagnosis and better outcomes compared to conventional methods in patients admitted with acute onset dyspnea.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications.
The abstract text does not report the primary source of funding. Funding information appears elsewhere in the manuscript but is not present in the abstract.
The protocol registration (PROSPERO CRD42021284070) is reported in the Methods section (text_5) but the abstract does not provide the register name or registration number.

elements.quote: There is an increasing body of evidence demonstrating that the accuracy of PoCUS is comparable to the current imaging reference standard CXR in general [16] as well as in specific conditions, such as pneumonia [17], acute decompensated heart failure [16], pleural effusion [18], pneumothorax [19] and pulmonary embolism [20]. PoCUS has other advantages, such as being free from ionizing radiation, and most importantly can be performed in real-time at the bedside [16, 21]. Additionally, PoCUS can answer a broad spectrum of remaining diagnostic questions and may also help to optimize and personalize therapy [22]. However, very few trials have examined meaningful clinical outcomes related to PoCUS usage to date [23] and the results on outcome measurements were heterogeneous [24].
elements.reason: The manuscript summarizes the current evidence on PoCUS diagnostic accuracy, its advantages, and explicitly notes gaps/uncertainties (few trials on clinical outcomes and heterogeneous results).

elements.quote: Acute-onset dyspnea is one of the most common symptoms for which patients visit the Emergency Department (ED) [1-4]. In the United States, dyspnea is the main reason for four to five million ED visits annually [4], representing up to 50% of patients admitted to acute tertiary care hospitals [5].... In addition to its high incidence, the 30-day mortality rate of these patients remains relatively high (8-13%) [7, 8]. Therefore, rapid and appropriate diagnosis of the underlying pathology is of utmost importance for prompt and adequate treatment [9]. ... Therefore, we conducted a high-quality, comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis that included the most recent publications that reported clinical outcomes with the use of PoCUS in patients who developed acute onset dyspnea.
elements.reason: The introduction states the high incidence and mortality of dyspnea and explains the need for rapid diagnosis, justifying why the review was conducted to assess PoCUS effects on clinical outcomes.

elements.quote: In contrast to previous reviews and meta-analyses [16-20, 60] that analyzed data from patients with an explicit diagnosis, such as pneumonia or acute decompensated heart failure [9, 10, 16, 17, 62], we applied a broader definition of dyspnea, thereby including more patients and providing more comprehensive results.
elements.reason: The authors contrast their review with previous reviews and explain the need for and added value of their broader approach. Additional support in text_21 notes prior reviews and that this review reports ED and ICU LOS as novel outcomes.

elements.quote: PoCUS has other advantages, such as being free from ionizing radiation, and most importantly can be performed in real-time at the bedside [16, 21]. Additionally, PoCUS can answer a broad spectrum of remaining diagnostic questions and may also help to optimize and personalize therapy [22].
elements.reason: The manuscript briefly describes how PoCUS works in practice (real-time bedside imaging, diagnostic breadth) and how that can lead to optimized/personalized therapy—constituting a brief proposed mechanism of action for the intervention.
No evidence (text or figure) was provided of a logic model or schematic showing hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes.

elements.quote: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of the use of Point-of-Care Ultrasound (PoCUS) versus conventional management on clinical outcomes in patients with acute onset dyspnea.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the review objective comparing PoCUS versus conventional management on clinical outcomes in patients with acute onset dyspnea; the Introduction similarly states the main objective to investigate how PoCUS improves clinical endpoints.

elements.quote: The selected studies had to match our previously defined PICO (Patients, Intervention, Control, Outcome) framework: ... P: Adults and children who were admitted to the ED or to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), or to another inpatient setting because of acute onset or worsening dyspnea ... I: The examined intervention was PoCUS use on its own or in combination with conventional diagnostic measures. ... C: Control group included conventional diagnostic methods, such as taking the patients' medical history, physical examination, ECG, blood gas and different laboratory analyses, echocardiography, CXR, or computer tomography (CT).
elements.reason: The review explicitly states the planned comparisons using a PICO framework with detailed descriptions of Patients, Intervention, and Control (and Outcomes elsewhere), satisfying the conditional requirement for intervention reviews.

elements.quote: The selected studies had to match our previously defined PICO (Patients, Intervention, Control, Outcome) framework: ... P: Adults and children who were admitted to the ED or to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), or to another inpatient setting because of acute onset or worsening dyspnea were eligible. We also included studies enrolling patients who developed shortness of breath from unknown etiologies and were already hospitalized. Studies reporting on trauma-induced acute onset dyspnea, or pregnancy were excluded. ... I: The examined intervention was PoCUS use on its own or in combination with conventional diagnostic measures. ... There were no restrictions on the type of PoCUS protocols. ... C: Control group included conventional diagnostic methods, such as taking the patients' medical history, physical examination, ECG, blood gas and different laboratory analyses, echocardiography, CXR, or computer tomography (CT).
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies PICO components (patients, intervention, control), eligible settings (ED, ICU, inpatient), populations included/excluded (e.g., trauma-induced dyspnea, pregnancy excluded), intervention details (PoCUS on its own or with conventional measures) and control definitions, satisfying specification of study characteristics used to determine eligibility.

elements.quote: We did not use any restrictions or limitations based on language or publication date.
elements.reason: The review explicitly states no restrictions on language or publication date. Additionally, selection criteria (text_6) exclude conference abstracts and non-peer-reviewed articles, indicating publication/report status restrictions were specified (e.g., exclusion of conference abstracts and non-peer-reviewed articles).
No information was provided distinguishing exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: C: Control group included conventional diagnostic methods, such as taking the patients' medical history, physical examination, ECG, blood gas and different laboratory analyses, echocardiography, CXR, or computer tomography (CT).
elements.reason: The review defines the groups used in syntheses (PoCUS intervention versus conventional diagnostic methods as control) and links them to comparisons evaluated in the review objectives.

Although some eligibility restrictions are listed (e.g., excluding trauma-induced dyspnea, pregnancy, certain study types), the manuscript does not provide explicit rationales explaining why these notable restrictions were applied.

elements.quote: We systematically searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) for eligible articles on 14 October, 2021.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the date (14 October, 2021) when the named electronic databases were searched.

elements.quote: We systematically searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) for eligible articles on 14 October, 2021.
elements.reason: Database names are provided and MEDLINE's interface is specified (via PubMed), but the search interface/platform is not specified for EMBASE or CENTRAL and no coverage dates (available date ranges) are reported.
No evidence that study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories searched are named or that any date restrictions for such sources are reported.

elements.quote: We also scanned the reference lists of included studies and the cited articles in Google Scholar.
elements.reason: An online source (Google Scholar) is named, but no URL is provided and no further details about search methods or other websites/engines with URLs are given.
There is no report of contacting organisations or manufacturers to identify studies or naming any such organisations.
No information is provided about contacting individuals (types of persons) to identify studies.

elements.quote: We also scanned the reference lists of included studies and the cited articles in Google Scholar.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state that they scanned reference lists of included studies (specifying the type of reference lists examined).

elements.quote: We also scanned the reference lists of included studies and the cited articles in Google Scholar.
elements.reason: The manuscript indicates forward/citation searching via 'cited articles in Google Scholar' (platform named), but does not report seed reports used for citation searching or the date the citation searching was performed.
No evidence that specific journals or conference proceedings consulted are named, nor that dates covered or search methods for such sources are reported.

No complete search strategies (the full search strings as actually run for each database) are provided in the retrieved evidence. The text refers to a 'detailed search key is outlined in the Additional Methods section' but that detailed strategy is not present in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: 'We systematically searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) for eligible articles on 14 October, 2021. We applied 'title, abstract, author, keyword' filters in EMBASE-no other filters were used. We did not use any restrictions or limitations based on language or publication date.'
elements.reason: Search limits and filters used are partially described (databases searched, date of search, EMBASE filters, and statement of no language/date restrictions). However, there is no justification of those limits by reference to eligibility criteria, nor are full search strings shown for each source.
No citation or description of published search approaches or filters and no description of adaptations in the provided evidence.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms in the provided evidence.
No information on tools used to translate search strings between sources is provided in the retrieved evidence.
No description of validation of the search strategy (process or validation studies) is present in the provided evidence.
No information is provided about any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) in the available evidence.
The evidence does not state whether the search structure was or was not based on PICO, nor does it describe a final conceptual structure or explorations used to develop a non-PICO structure.

elements.quote: After the removal of duplicates using a reference management software (EndNote X9, Clarivate Analytics), two review authors (G.S. and C.S.) independently screened titles, abstracts, and then the full texts against predefined eligibility criteria.
elements.reason: Explicitly states that two reviewers (G.S. and C.S.) screened titles/abstracts and full texts.

elements.quote: two review authors (G.S. and C.S.) independently screened titles, abstracts, and then the full texts against predefined eligibility criteria.
elements.reason: Clearly reports that the two reviewers screened independently.

elements.quote: Discrepancies were resolved by two other review authors (Z.M. and M.R.).
elements.reason: Describes how screening disagreements were resolved (by two other named review authors).

elements.quote: In the case of one study (Blans [46]), the author kindly provided the original data on patients with dyspnea, excluding all other causes.
elements.reason: Reports that the authors obtained original data from a study investigator to clarify eligibility/data, describing a process of obtaining information from study authors.
No information is provided about methods used to translate abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.

elements.quote: After the removal of duplicates using a reference management software (EndNote X9, Clarivate Analytics)...
elements.reason: Describes use of an automation tool (EndNote X9) to remove duplicates as part of the selection process.
No information about externally derived classifiers, their versions/references, roles, or records removed before screening is reported.
No information about internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use is provided.
No description of machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules is provided.
No information about use or integration of crowdsourcing platforms in study selection is reported.
No description of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or how they were derived is provided.

elements.quote: Data on the first author, publication year, countries, study design, number of patients in each group and their baseline characteristics (including age and gender), type of PoCUS protocol, examiners' practice and the available primary and secondary outcome parameters were extracted by two independent review authors (G.S. and C.S.) using our standardized data collection form in Microsoft Excel.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports that two reviewers (G.S. and C.S.) extracted data from reports.

elements.quote: two review authors (G.S. and C.S.) independently screened titles, abstracts, and then the full texts against predefined eligibility criteria.... Data ... were extracted by two independent review authors (G.S. and C.S.) using our standardized data collection form in Microsoft Excel.
elements.reason: The text states that two data collectors worked independently for screening and data extraction.

elements.quote: Discrepancies were resolved by two other review authors (Z.M. and M.R.).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes a process to resolve disagreements: unresolved discrepancies were resolved by two other named review authors.

elements.reason: The authors report at least one instance where they obtained original data directly from a study author, describing a process of obtaining data from investigators.

No description of automation tools used for data collection (use, training, or validation) is provided in the retrieved evidence. EndNote and Excel are mentioned for deduplication and data entry but not as data-collection automation tools with details.
The retrieved evidence does not report any methods used to translate articles for data collection.

elements.quote: extracting numerical data from figures was particularly difficult,
elements.reason: While the authors note difficulty extracting numerical data from figures, they do not specify any software used to extract data from figures.

elements.quote: There were no overlapping populations or duplicate data.
elements.reason: The manuscript states there were no overlapping or duplicate populations and mentions use of a standardized data collection form and estimation methods for means/SDs from medians (text_8), but it does not provide explicit decision rules for selecting among multiple reports or detailed procedures for resolving inconsistent data across reports.

elements.quote: Time to diagnosis was the most cited endpoint in the studies (7 of 15). PoCUS use compared to controls resulted in a significant reduction in time to making the diagnosis (MD - 63 min; 95% CI - 115 to - 11 min) ... Time to treatment was reported in four studies. ... As far as in-hospital LOS is concerned, PoCUS use showed no significant effect (MD - 0.02 days; 95% CI - 0.43 to 0.39 days) ... Regarding LOS in the ED, there was a mean of 35 min less waiting time ... Patients in the PoCUS group stayed for a significantly shorter time in the ICU than controls (MD - 1.27 days; 95% CI - 1.94 to - 0.61 days).
elements.reason: Multiple outcome domains (time to diagnosis, time to treatment, in-hospital LOS, ED LOS, ICU LOS) are listed and reported with units and effect estimates, but the manuscript does not provide formal definitions for each outcome domain or a comprehensive list/definition of all outcomes sought (e.g., primary vs secondary pre-specified definitions), so this is partial.

elements.quote: Time to diagnosis ... (MD - 63 min; 95% CI - 115 to - 11 min). Time to treatment was reported in four studies. ... in-hospital LOS ... (MD - 0.02 days; 95% CI - 0.43 to 0.39 days). Regarding LOS in the ED, there was a mean of 35 min less waiting time ... Patients in the PoCUS group stayed for a significantly shorter time in the ICU ... (MD - 1.27 days; 95% CI - 1.94 to - 0.61 days).
elements.reason: The time frames/units of measurement for outcomes are specified in the text (minutes for time to diagnosis/treatment and ED LOS, days for in-hospital and ICU LOS; 30-day endpoints are reported elsewhere), so the measurement time frames are provided.
No statement was found describing whether the authors sought all results compatible with each outcome domain (for all measures, time points, analyses) or not.
There is no description of a process used to select specific results when not all compatible results were sought.

elements.quote: The protocol was prospectively registered via the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number CRD42021284070. There was no deviation from the protocol.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports protocol registration and explicitly states there were no deviations from the protocol, thereby reporting changes to outcome-domain inclusion (none) with rationale.

elements.quote: The protocol was prospectively registered via the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number CRD42021284070. There was no deviation from the protocol.
elements.reason: Authors state prospectively registered protocol and that there were no deviations, which reports that there were no changes to processes for selecting results.
No statement was found identifying which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions or providing a rationale for prioritisation.

elements.quote: Based on the consensus of methodological and clinical experts, we created a standardized data collection sheet. Data on the first author, publication year, countries, study design, number of patients in each group and their baseline characteristics (including age and gender), type of PoCUS protocol, examiners' practice and the available primary and secondary outcome parameters were extracted by two independent review authors (G.S. and C.S.) using our standardized data collection form in Microsoft Excel.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the additional variables sought (author, year, country, study design, patient numbers and baseline characteristics including age and gender, PoCUS protocol, examiners' practice, primary and secondary outcomes) and states they used a standardized data collection sheet.

elements.quote: If the mean and SD were not reported in the article, we estimated them from the medians, quartiles, minimum and maximums using the Luo [32] and Shi [33] methods.
elements.reason: The authors describe how they handled missing summary data (estimating means and SDs from medians/quartiles/min/max using cited methods), which documents assumptions/procedures for missing or unclear information.

elements.quote: Based on the consensus of methodological and clinical experts, we created a standardized data collection sheet.
elements.reason: While a standardized data collection sheet is mentioned, no specific tool, checklist, or citation for a tool used to determine which data items to collect is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: For RCTs the RoB 2 tool (revised tool for Risk of Bias in randomized trials) was used, whereas for the cohorts, we used the ROBINS-I tool (Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions) [27, 28].
elements.reason: The text explicitly names the risk-of-bias tools used (RoB 2 for RCTs and ROBINS-I for cohort studies).

elements.quote: The risk of bias was assessed based on the recommendations of the Cochrane Collaboration.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that assessments followed Cochrane recommendations (and names the tools), but does not list the specific domains, components, or items from RoB 2 or ROBINS-I in the provided text (detailed description is deferred to Additional Tables).

elements.quote: Based on the Cochrane proposal, the risk of bias assessment showed serious concern for only one article [48] and moderate (some concern in cases of RCTs) or low risk for all others.
elements.reason: The authors report overall risk-of-bias judgments for individual studies (serious, moderate/some concern, or low), but they do not describe the explicit rules or criteria used to derive these overall judgments in the provided evidence.
No information in the provided text indicates any adaptations made to existing risk-of-bias tools.

elements.quote: For RCTs the RoB 2 tool (revised tool for Risk of Bias in randomized trials) was used, whereas for the cohorts, we used the ROBINS-I tool (Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions) [27, 28].
elements.reason: The authors used established, named risk-of-bias tools (RoB 2 and ROBINS-I); there is no indication a newly developed tool was created, so this item does not apply.

elements.quote: Two independent review authors (G.S. and C.S.) did the assessment, and an independent third investigator resolved any disagreements (F.D.).
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (two), that they worked independently, and the method for resolving disagreements (an independent third investigator) are all explicitly reported.

No description is provided of processes used to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators (no contact or request procedures for investigators are reported in the supplied evidence).
The provided evidence does not describe any use of automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, or validation).

elements.quote: If there were at least three studies for an outcome, a metaanalysis was performed, and the results displayed in forest plots. For continuous outcomes, pooled mean differences (MDs), and for dichotomous variables, pooled odds ratios (ORs) along with their 95% confidence interval (CI), were calculated to investigate the differences between the compared arms. A random effect model was used for meta-analyses. Time to diagnosis was the most cited endpoint in the studies (7 of 15). PoCUS use compared to controls resulted in a significant reduction in time to making the diagnosis (MD - 63 min; 95% CI - 115 to - 11 min) (Fig. 2A). Time to treatment was reported in four studies. In the PoCUS group, patients also received treatment significantly earlier (MD - 27 min; 95% CI - 43 to - 11 min) compared to controls (Fig. 2B). Heterogeneity among these trials for both outcomes was considerable ( I 2 = 100%, p = 0 and 88%, p < 0.01, respectively). If the study number for the given outcome was over five, the Hartung-Knapp adjustment [30, 31] was applied. ... As far as in-hospital LOS is concerned, PoCUS use showed no significant effect (MD - 0.02 days; 95% CI - 0.43 to 0.39 days), with low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%, p = 0.81). Regarding LOS in the ED, there was a mean of 35 min less waiting time to discharge or admission to a ward that proved not significant (MD - 35 min; 95% CI - 93 to 23 min), but heterogeneity was high ( I 2 = 84%, p < 0.01). Patients in the PoCUS group stayed for a significantly shorter time in the ICU than controls (MD - 1.27 days; 95% CI - 1.94 to - 0.61 days) (Fig. 2C). Heterogeneity was moderate among these trials ( I 2 = 46%, p = 0.16). To estimate the heterogeneity variance measure, τ 2 was applied estimated with the Q profile method.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports results of multiple pre-specified statistical syntheses (meta-analyses) across primary and secondary outcomes, including pooled MDs and ORs and associated heterogeneity assessments.

elements.quote: Regarding secondary endpoints, patients in the PoCUS group had significantly higher odds (OR 2.31; 95% CI 1.61 to 3.32) of receiving appropriate therapy compared to controls, and studies showed low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%, p = 0.67) (Fig. 3A). We found no significant effects on 30-day re-admission rate (OR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.56 to 1.17) with low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%, p = 0.78); 30-day mortality (OR, 0.82; 95% CI 0.31-2.18) and in-hospital mortality (OR 0.62; 95% CI 0.37 to 1.04), with moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 50%, p = 0.11 and I 2 = 37%, p = 0.16, respectively) (Fig. 3 and Additional Fig. 1).

Furthermore, the final GRADE assessment is also shown in Additional Table 1.
elements.reason: No explicit explanations or reasons for rating certainty down or up (e.g., specific GRADE domains and justifications) are provided in the retrieved evidence; only a general statement and a reference to supplementary material are given.

elements.quote: In contrast to previous reviews and meta-analyses [16-20, 60] that analyzed data from patients with an explicit diagnosis, such as pneumonia or acute decompensated heart failure [9, 10, 16, 17, 62], we applied a broader definition of dyspnea, thereby including more patients and providing more comprehensive results.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly interpret their results relative to prior reviews and meta-analyses, describing differences in inclusion criteria and how their broader definition affects comprehensiveness—placing their findings in the context of existing evidence.

elements.quote: Our results are in contrast with a recently published guideline [61], which states that clinicians may use PoCUS in addition to the standard diagnostic pathway when there is diagnostic uncertainty. Based on our results, we recommend that all patients suffering from acute onset dyspnea should be managed by PoCUS as a standard and not only as a supplementary tool when standard diagnostic measures fail.
elements.reason: The authors compare their findings to a recent guideline and other systematic reviews, highlighting agreements and contrasts and making recommendations based on that comparison, thereby interpreting results in the context of other evidence.

elements.quote: Our study also has certain limitations. There was substantial heterogeneity regarding the age groups as we included infants and patients older than 59 years [40, 47]. Severity of illness, as indicated by the patients' different medical conditions, also showed heterogeneity as some articles included intubated, mechanically ventilated patients, while others excluded this group [41, 47]. Furthermore, not all patients had dyspnea only as the sole complaint. Some articles also included patients with coughing or chest pain, which further increased the heterogeneity of the study population (Table 1). ... The diversity of PoCUS protocols may be another important factor behind the high heterogeneity of the results and this is a key point and limitation at the same time, from both the methodological and clinical points of view. For example, some studies used PoCUS only to investigate the lungs, whereas others examined the heart or both heart and lungs, while some studies also evaluated the venous system (Table 1). Furthermore, there is a lack of standardization regarding PoCUS training and practice. Hence, we cannot exclude that in this regard there was substantial diversity in the included studies.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly describes multiple limitations of the included evidence — substantial heterogeneity in age groups and illness severity, inclusion of patients with mixed complaints, variability in PoCUS protocols, and lack of standardization in training/practice.

elements.quote: Our study also has certain limitations. There was substantial heterogeneity regarding the age groups as we included infants and patients older than 59 years [40, 47]. Severity of illness, as indicated by the patients' different medical conditions, also showed heterogeneity as some articles included intubated, mechanically ventilated patients, while others excluded this group [41, 47]. Furthermore, not all patients had dyspnea only as the sole complaint. Some articles also included patients with coughing or chest pain, which further increased the heterogeneity of the study population (Table 1). ... The diversity of PoCUS protocols may be another important factor behind the high heterogeneity of the results and this is a key point and limitation at the same time, from both the methodological and clinical points of view. ... Furthermore, there is a lack of standardization regarding PoCUS training and practice. Hence, we cannot exclude that in this regard there was substantial diversity in the included studies. ... Additionally, there were also some challenges in the interpretation of the reported data. For example, extracting numerical data from figures was particularly difficult, and in one case [48] the re-admission rate period was 21 days instead of 30 days. ... On the other hand, classification of the primary and secondary end points was arbitrarily defined by us at the time of the PROSPERO registration. This was followed throughout the analysis and not modified subsequently, although not all articles used exactly the same classification as we did.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly lists multiple limitations of the review processes (heterogeneity in age and illness severity, inclusion criteria variability, diversity of PoCUS protocols, lack of standardization in training, data extraction challenges, and endpoint classification).

elements.quote: There was substantial heterogeneity regarding the age groups ... Severity of illness ... also showed heterogeneity ... some articles also included patients with coughing or chest pain, which further increased the heterogeneity of the study population (Table 1). However, we tried to overcome this issue by including studies where the majority of subjects required medical intervention for acute onset dyspnea and included them in data collection and analysis. The diversity of PoCUS protocols may be another important factor behind the high heterogeneity of the results and this is a key point and limitation at the same time, from both the methodological and clinical points of view. ... Furthermore, there is a lack of standardization regarding PoCUS training and practice. Hence, we cannot exclude that in this regard there was substantial diversity in the included studies. ... extracting numerical data from figures was particularly difficult, and in one case [48] the re-admission rate period was 21 days instead of 30 days. ... On the other hand, classification of the primary and secondary end points was arbitrarily defined by us at the time of the PROSPERO registration. This was followed throughout the analysis and not modified subsequently, although not all articles used exactly the same classification as we did. ... these limitations highlight the importance and need for the development of gold standards for the management of this patient population to improve quality of care.
elements.reason: The Discussion not only lists limitations but explains their potential impacts (e.g., increased heterogeneity of study populations and results, influence of protocol and training diversity on findings, data extraction issues affecting outcome measures, and arbitrary endpoint classification potentially affecting analyses), and notes attempts to mitigate some issues.

elements.quote: The results of this systematic review and meta-analysis indicate that all patients admitted with acute onset dyspnea should be examined with PoCUS to reduce time to diagnosis, time to treatment, LOS and potentially mortality.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly states a practice implication recommending that all patients with acute onset dyspnea be examined with PoCUS to improve clinical outcomes.

elements.quote: Our results are in contrast with a recently published guideline [61], which states that clinicians may use PoCUS in addition to the standard diagnostic pathway when there is diagnostic uncertainty. Based on our results, we recommend that all patients suffering from acute onset dyspnea should be managed by PoCUS as a standard and not only as a supplementary tool when standard diagnostic measures fail.
elements.reason: The authors contrast their findings with an existing guideline and explicitly recommend changing management standards—i.e., a policy-level recommendation to adopt PoCUS as standard care.

elements.quote: There are several positive signals in our results that should encourage further research in this field. To optimize PoCUS use in daily routine, further studies are needed in which patient selection criteria provide a more homogeneous population, and the experience of the examiners is also well defined. Finally, standardizing PoCUS protocols is of paramount importance and is a challenging task for the future. ... According to our results, PoCUS use may reduce LOS in ED and the ICU, which could have other potential beneficial effects (e.g., decreased costs and/or reduced emergency room wait times) that should be investigated in future.
elements.reason: The Discussion provides explicit recommendations for future research, identifying specific areas (patient selection, examiner experience, protocol standardization, and investigation of cost/operational impacts) to be addressed.
